content.title: About
content.content: Bread, onion, toasted is a slice of whole‑grain bread topped with golden, caramelized onion rings. The onions are fried until sweet and crisp, creating a perfect contrast with the crunchy bread crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Toasted onion is a common garnish in many world cuisines, adding both flavor and texture.
Caramelization of onions occurs above 120 °C, turning sugars into aromatic compounds.
The bread‑onion combo was a staple for medieval travelers as a simple, filling snack.
Onions contain quercetin, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after heating.
Bread with toasted onion is often served alongside soups and salads as a hearty appetizer.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Onion adds vitamin C, which helps maintain a strong immune system.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Quercetin and other compounds in onion help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and antioxidants contribute to lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Bread supplies quick‑release carbohydrates, while onion adds a modest amount of protein.

items.title: Onion allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to onion, ranging from mild skin irritation to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If the onions are seasoned with salt, the dish may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gastric irritation
items.content: Toasted onion can aggravate the stomach lining in people prone to acid reflux or gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the toasted onion bread as a snack with soups, salads, or as a quick open‑face sandwich. Add cheese, avocado, or fresh herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, store bread and toasted onions separately and reheat in the oven before serving.

pizza-with-meat-whole-wheat-thick-crust.title: Meat Pizza, Whole Wheat Thick Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Meat pizza on a whole wheat thick crust combines a savory tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, a variety of meat toppings (ham, sausage, beef) and a crunchy, nutrient‑rich crust made from whole‑grain flour. This pizza offers a rich meat flavor together with the benefits of whole grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat crust provides more fiber and micronutrients than a standard white crust.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are high in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Meat toppings often include lean beef pieces, boosting the protein content.
Pizza originated in Naples, but today its variations are adapted to local tastes worldwide.
A thick crust retains more moisture, making each bite juicier.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat and cheese supply high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Fiber from whole grains
items.content: Whole wheat flour increases dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole grains contain B1, B3, B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, helping protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Mozzarella provides calcium and phosphorus important for bones and teeth.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The thick crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Processed meat toppings can contain saturated fats that may affect cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salty meats and cheese increase sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole wheat flour contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Potential additives
items.content: Some pre‑made meat toppings may contain preservatives; choose fresh ingredients when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pizza into serving pieces and enjoy it hot. Adding fresh vegetables such as arugula or cherry tomatoes after baking enhances flavor and adds vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the crust crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Wild rice is the seed of the aquatic grass Zizania, native to freshwater lakes and rivers of North America. Despite its name, it is not true rice but a grain with a nutty flavor and a slightly chewy texture when cooked. It is commonly used in salads, side dishes, and Asian-inspired recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild rice contains more protein and fiber than regular white rice.
It was considered a "superfood" by Native American tribes and featured in ceremonial dishes.
Harvesting of wild rice in the wild is regulated to protect natural populations.
In the United States, wild rice is officially classified as a cereal crop, though botanically it is an aquatic grass.
It has a lower glycemic index than most rice varieties.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Wild rice provides about 14 g of protein per 100 g, making it a solid plant‑based protein source.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains virtually no fat, suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Provides magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, and iron, essential for metabolism and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Contains phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to wild rice.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: In some growing regions, wild rice can accumulate arsenic; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: High fiber intake may cause bloating in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook wild rice in a 1:3 rice‑to‑water ratio for 45‑55 minutes until tender. It can be added to salads, soups, casseroles, used as a side dish for fish or meat, or prepared as a risotto.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store uncooked wild rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 3‑4 days.
